paragraphs.text: GPS clocks gain 38 microseconds a day from relativity.
Start with the assumption. Navigation falls back to other sources, while timing-dependent networks start to drift.
That is the first effect — but not the biggest. Assume GPS signals stopped for a day.

The second-order effect is stranger. GPS clocks gain 38 microseconds a day from relativity. Without correction, positions would drift quickly. The system became fully operational in 1993. It was designed around 24 satellites. Civil accuracy reached about 5 metres. If it went dark, phones would lean on cell towers and Wi-Fi. But networks and markets that use GPS timing would feel it too. So GPS isn't just maps. It's the world's shared clock. Relativity predicted that the clocks on GPS satellites, as observed by those on Earth, run 38 microseconds faster per day than those on the Earth. The prototype spacecraft was launched in 1978 and the full constellation of 24 satellites became operational in 1993. When Selective Availability was discontinued, GPS was accurate to about 5 meters (16 ft). As of March 2026, 21 GPS satellites broadcast L5 signals. GPS receivers compute position from precise satellite clock signals, which also serve as a timing reference. GPS signals stopped for a day.
And here is where science stops being certain. The governing physics: GPS receivers compute position from precise satellite clock signals, which also serve as a timing reference.
So what is the answer? The exact timeline depends on how the impossible change happens; the order of effects is what established physics constrains.
